newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. seen unlikely to respond to pressure at summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen unlikely to respond to pressure at summit.

text.p: The United States is under heavy attack at the U.N. Earth Summit from both Europe and the Third World but delegates said on Wednesday they were not hopeful of concessions by President Bill Clinton.
Clinton addresses the 173-nation conference on Thursday.
"It would be a surprise if he had some concrete message on climate change, on finances, on transferring technology to developing countries," said Norwegian Environment Minister Torbjoern Berntsen.
"If the industrial countries don't help we are not moving forward. But I am afraid he won't say anything like that."

Once the world's leader on environmental issues, the United States has faced steady criticism, from Europe for refusing to set targets to cut global warming, and from developing nations for reducing aid.
The week-long summit will end on Friday with a lengthy document giving guidelines for the environment and development in the 21th century.

Some Third World countries on Wednesday blocked a text on climate change, hoping that Clinton would give specific targets for curbing carbon emissions from coal, oil and other fossil fuels that cause global warming.

"The big question is whether one should begin negotiations after Clinton has spoken in hopes he will go further than in the Denver Group of Seven summit," said Michaele Hustedt, a German delegation member.
"But the entire German delegation disagrees," she said, "because he will not go further."
In Denver Clinton resisted European pressure to set specific targets on cutting the greenhouse gases.

Despite the controversy over global warming, the main emphasis of most developing states was on issues like clean water, soil erosion, arid lands, marine ecosystems -- and financing for environmentally-safe development.
"The South feels, correctly, that sacrificing growth will only perpetuate injustice," said Singaporean Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong.

"It is unfair to expect the poor to bear the main costs of reducing global environmental risks, especially when most of those risks are attributable to past actions by today's affluent countries," he said.
He added: "Without adequate funding, sustainable development is only a slogan."

Most rich countries agreed in principle in Rio to increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of their gross national product. But since then it has decreased from 0.35 percent to 0.27 percent in 1995, with the United States registering the sharpest drop.

Clinton has rejected pressure to set specific targets to control carbon emissions from oil, coal and other fuels. The United States is by far the world's largest polluter of so-called greenhouse gases followed by China, Russia, Japan and Germany.

The disputes at the meeting go beyond global warming. Some Europeans also want the final summit document to call for a global tax on international aviation fuel, a treaty protecting the world's forests and a world energy strategy to reduce use of oil, coal and other fossil fuels.
All these positions are opposed by Washington.
As an indication of difficulties, the White House on Wednesday announced strict new proposals to lower the 0.12 parts-per-million standard for smog-forming ozone to 0.08 parts-per-million.
But Democrats and Republicans from U.S industrial states said they would try to derail the new air standards, meant to curb respiratory illnesses, saying the measures are too costly to implement.
"I can tell you ... we will go to war, we cannot survive," said Representative Ron Klink, a Pennsylvania Democrat.
